vocabulary.meaning: the state of not having a job while wanting and being able to work
examples: Youth unemployment remains high in some countries.
Long-term unemployment can damage confidence.

vocabulary.meaning: the system in which employers look for workers and people look for jobs
examples: Graduates are entering a difficult job market.
Digital skills are increasingly valuable in the job market.

vocabulary.meaning: a person who has completed a university or college course
examples: Many graduates struggle to find their first job.
The company recruits new graduates every year.

vocabulary.meaning: a programme that combines paid work with practical training
examples: An apprenticeship can provide valuable work experience.
The government is expanding apprenticeship opportunities.

vocabulary.meaning: a difference between the skills employers need and the skills workers have
examples: Training programmes can reduce the skills gap.
Employers say the skills gap makes recruitment harder.

vocabulary.meaning: suitable for someone starting a career with little experience
examples: She applied for several entry-level jobs.
Entry-level salaries vary widely by industry.

vocabulary.meaning: practical experience gained by doing a job or placement
examples: Employers often ask young applicants for work experience.
Internships can provide useful work experience.

vocabulary.meaning: a situation in which someone works fewer hours than desired or in a job below their skill level
examples: Many young workers experience underemployment.
Underemployment can hide problems in the labour market.

vocabulary.meaning: the opportunities someone has for future progress in their career
examples: Training improved his career prospects.
Young people may move abroad for better career prospects.

vocabulary.meaning: a period when economic activity becomes weaker
examples: Youth unemployment often rises during an economic downturn.
The recession created a severe economic downturn.
